newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Fourth Australian rate cut possible early '97.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Fourth Australian rate cut possible early '97.

text.p: Caught off-guard on Wednesday by the surprise central bank announcement of a half percent interest rate cut, Australian markets are already focusing on whether there is room for another monetary policy easing in early 1997.

With inflation seen remaining well-behaved, analysts said the key to whether the official cash rate moves from the current level of 6.0 percent will be activity indicators, and the performance of the Australian dollar.
"Based on our expectations for growth and inflation, another move down in interest rates is certainly quite possible," ANZ Securities chief economist Philip Graham said.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) announced the half percent cut in the official cash rate to 6.0 percent to an unsuspecting market on Wednesday morning, following similar-sized cuts on July 31 and November 6.

RBA governor Ian Macfarlane cited the further improvement in the inflationary outlook as being behind the rate cut, with the recent strength of the Australian dollar being supportive of the low inflation environment.

"Overall it is the Bank's assessment that the economy has the capacity to grow a little faster without putting pressure on inflation," Macfarlane said, adding that the three cuts should help employment growth, subject to wage restraint.
It was this view that led many to expect a further rate cut.
"Today's rate cut does not rule out further cuts in interest rates," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said.
"If the Aussie remains strong, and inflation expectations continue to fall, the RBA will cut again," he said.
For many, a third condition that has to be met is for the labour market to remain subdued well into 1997.

"If employment shows no signs of a substantive pick up by around the June quarter 1997, then the RBA track record would suggest further easings are probable," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
Australian unemployment has stalled around 8.5 percent over the past 18 months or so, and it was a key factor in each of the two previous cuts in interest rates.
Data released last week showed economic growth running at 3.8 percent, leaving analysts to think the RBA must be aiming for four percent plus growth to reduce unemployment.

Commonwealth Bank economists said a lesson from the cut was that "provided the RBA is comfortable with the inflation outlook it will take the opportunity to nudge the economy on to a stronger growth path, consistent with its employment objective".
And the RBA appears to be comfortable with the near term inflation outlook, economists said.

"The Bank now expects underlying inflation to stay below 2.5 percent for the remainder of this financial year, and our assessment is for continued good inflation performance in 1997/98," Macfarlane said in the statement announcing the cut.
But others felt that the policy easing cycle had come to an end and further cuts in 1997 would risk fuelling an economy that was expected to be growing stronger by itself.
"My view is that it is the end of the easing cycle," Rothschild Australia chief economist Ric Simes said.
"I think that the Bank would be wary about cutting in the New Year again because of the risk of it being pro-cyclical."
While most of the debate was on whether there would be a fourth rate cut, some felt the third move was unnecessary, and may require remedial action next year.
"We suspect this one will lead to near boom conditions in the economy in 1997," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
"Indeed this cut may be the one that proves to be one too many."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
